title: The Importance of Cells
seo_title: Grade 11 General Science: The Importance of Cells Worksheets (Strengthened SHS)
standard_code: Grade 11 General Science, Term 2: Chemistry and life science
standard_text: The importance of cells in living things: prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, organelles and their functions, the microscope, and movement of substances across membranes. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, General Science, Term 2)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 General Science worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Term 2): prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, organelles and their functions, microscopy and magnification, membranes and transport and surface area to volume ratio. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Convert to the same unit first: 1 mm = 1,000 µm.
body_html:
How to think about it

Prokaryotic cells (bacteria, archaea) have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells do. Organelles divide the work: mitochondria release energy, ribosomes make proteins, chloroplasts photosynthesize.

The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins (fluid mosaic model). Substances cross by diffusion, osmosis (water), facilitated diffusion, active transport (needs ATP) and endo- or exocytosis.

As a cell gets bigger its surface area to volume ratio falls, so exchange becomes too slow; that is why cells are small.

Example

An image 30 mm long shows a cell 15 µm long. Magnification?

30 mm = 30 000 µm

30 000 ÷ 15

Answer: ×2000

Example

Cube with 2 cm sides: SA:V?

SA = 6 × 4 = 24 cm²

V = 8 cm³

24 ÷ 8

Answer: 3 : 1

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to convert mm to µm before dividing.
  • Saying water moves by osmosis towards the more dilute solution: it moves to the more concentrated one.
  • Calling active transport ‘diffusion with energy’: it moves substances against the gradient.

faq.q: What is the difference between osmosis and diffusion?
faq.a: Both are passive. Osmosis is the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane; diffusion can be any particle.

faq.q: Why do large cells have trouble exchanging materials?
faq.a: Volume increases faster than surface area, so each unit of volume has less membrane for exchange.

items.q: What is active transport?
c: movement down a gradient with no energy
movement against a concentration gradient using carrier proteins and ATP
items.e: Root hair cells take up mineral ions this way.

items.q: Why can oxygen diffuse straight through the phospholipid bilayer?
items.e: Ions need channel proteins.

items.q: What happens in anaphase of mitosis?
c: sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles
items.e: The centromeres divide.

items.q: What happens to a red blood cell in pure water?
c: water enters by osmosis and it bursts
items.e: Animal cells have no cell wall.

items.q: Which factor increases the rate of diffusion?
items.e: Fick's law: rate ∝ area × difference ÷ thickness.

items.q: What is facilitated diffusion?
c: passive movement of molecules through channel or carrier proteins
items.e: Down a concentration gradient.

items.q: Which organelle is the site of aerobic respiration?
items.e: Mitochondria make most of the cell's ATP.

items.q: What is the main function of mitochondria?
c: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)
items.e: Mitochondria: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell).

items.q: Why is a virus not considered a living cell?
c: it has no cytoplasm or ribosomes and can only replicate inside a host cell
items.e: Viruses are acellular.

items.q: A nucleus is 6.00 µm long. How long will its image be, in mm, at a magnification of ×20,000?
items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 120,000 µm = 120 mm.

items.q: In ultracentrifugation, which organelle forms the first pellet?
items.e: The heaviest organelles settle at the lowest speed.

items.q: Which microscope has the highest resolution?
items.e: Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light.

items.q: A pollen grain is 25.0 µm long. How long will its image be, in mm, at a magnification of ×5,000?
items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 125,000 µm = 125 mm.

items.q: In a photograph a mitochondrion is 40.0 mm long. The magnification is ×20,000. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 40.0 mm ÷ 20,000 = 0.00200 mm = 2.00 µm.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for giving color to fruits and flowers?
items.e: Chromoplasts: giving color to fruits and flowers.

items.q: What are the ribosomes of prokaryotes?
items.e: Mitochondria and chloroplasts also have 70S ribosomes.

items.q: A nucleus is 6.00 µm long. How long will its image be, in mm, at a magnification of ×1,000?
items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 6,000 µm = 6.00 mm.

items.q: What happens in interphase?
c: chromosomes line up at the equator
DNA replicates and the cell grows
items.e: Organelles are also copied.

items.q: What is the main function of chloroplasts?
c: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)
items.e: Chloroplasts: photosynthesis.

items.q: A cheek cell is 80.0 µm long. How long will its image be, in mm, at a magnification of ×1,500?
items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 120,000 µm = 120 mm.

items.q: Which part of the cell is the largest cell in the human body?
items.e: The longest cell is the nerve cell.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for digesting materials with hydrolytic enzymes?
items.e: Lysosomes: digesting materials with hydrolytic enzymes.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)?
items.e: Mitochondria: the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell).

items.q: What is the main function of centrioles?
c: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
items.e: Centrioles: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia.

items.q: What is the main function of nucleolus?
c: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
items.e: Nucleolus: making ribosomal RNA.

items.q: What is the main function of rough endoplasmic reticulum?
c: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
items.e: Rough endoplasmic reticulum: making and secreting proteins.

items.q: What is the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane?
c: a lipid bilayer in which proteins float, with the lipid able to move sideways
items.e: Proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972).

items.q: What is a metacentric chromosome?
c: one with the centromere in the middle and two equal arms
one with the centromere at the end
items.e: Telocentric chromosomes have a terminal centromere.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for photosynthesis?
items.e: Chloroplasts: photosynthesis.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for making ribosomal RNA?
items.e: Nucleolus: making ribosomal RNA.

items.q: What does the 'S' in 70S ribosome stand for?
c: the Svedberg unit, a measure of sedimentation
items.e: It depends on size and shape.

items.q: A scale bar 20 mm long represents 50 µm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
What is the main function of leucoplasts?
items.e: Leucoplasts: storing starch, oils and proteins.

items.q: Which organelle is responsible for storing starch, oils and proteins?
items.e: Leucoplasts: storing starch, oils and proteins.

items.q: A guard cell is 30.0 µm long. How long will its image be, in mm, at a magnification of ×10,000?
items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 300,000 µm = 300 mm.

items.q: A chloroplast is 6.00 µm long. How long will its image be, in mm, at a magnification of ×5,000?
items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 30,000 µm = 30.0 mm.

items.q: What is the main function of vacuole?
c: forming the spindle during animal cell division and the bases of cilia
giving color to fruits and flowers
storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid
items.e: Vacuole: storing water, sap and waste, and keeping the cell turgid.

items.q: In a photograph a red blood cell is 150 mm long. The magnification is ×20,000. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 150 mm ÷ 20,000 = 0.00750 mm = 7.50 µm.

items.q: What is the main function of Golgi apparatus?
c: packaging and secretion of materials, and forming glycoproteins and glycolipids
the site of aerobic respiration (the powerhouse of the cell)
items.e: Golgi apparatus: packaging and secretion of materials, and forming glycoproteins and glycolipids.

items.q: Cell X has a water potential of −500 kPa and cell Y has −1000 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−500 kPa) is higher.

items.q: Which process moves large particles out of a cell in vesicles?
items.e: Vesicles fuse with the membrane to release their contents.

items.q: Which statement compares prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells correctly?
c: only eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
items.e: Both have a membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.

items.q: Why is cell fractionation done in an ice-cold, isotonic, buffered solution?
c: to stop enzymes working, stop osmosis damaging organelles and keep pH constant
items.e: Then the homogenate is filtered and centrifuged.

items.q: Which structure is found in plant cells but not animal cells?
items.e: Plant cells also have chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

items.q: How do prokaryotic cells divide?
items.e: The circular DNA and plasmids are copied first.

items.q: What is the function of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
items.e: It has no ribosomes.

items.q: A root hair cell has a water potential of −350 kPa and the soil water has −800 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from a root hair cell to the soil water
from the soil water to a root hair cell
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: A red blood cell is placed in pure water. What happens?
c: the cell wall stops it bursting
water leaves and the cell shrinks
water enters by osmosis and the cell may burst
items.e: Animal cells have no cell wall.

items.q: Cell A has a water potential of −400 kPa and cell B has −1200 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from cell B to cell A
from cell A to cell B
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: How does a white blood cell take in a bacterium?
items.e: The membrane surrounds the particle.

items.q: Cell X has a water potential of −1000 kPa and cell Y has −700 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−700 kPa) is higher.

items.q: What is the fluid mosaic model?
c: a layer of DNA around the cell
a phospholipid bilayer with proteins that can move within it
items.e: Proteins float in a fluid bilayer.

items.q: A potato cell has a water potential of −350 kPa and the sucrose solution has −500 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−350 kPa) is higher.

items.q: A root hair cell has a water potential of −1200 kPa and the soil water has −1000 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−1000 kPa) is higher.

items.q: An onion cell has a water potential of −150 kPa and the salt solution has −600 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−150 kPa) is higher.

items.q: What is facilitated diffusion?
c: passive movement through channel or carrier proteins
items.e: Glucose and ions often need protein channels.

items.q: Cell X has a water potential of −800 kPa and cell Y has −150 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from cell Y to cell X
from cell X to cell Y
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: A potato cell has a water potential of −150 kPa and the sucrose solution has −1200 kPa. In which direction does water move by osmosis?
c: from a potato cell to the sucrose solution
from the sucrose solution to a potato cell
items.e: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) water potential.

items.q: What is diffusion?
c: movement of large particles in vesicles
net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration
movement against a concentration gradient using ATP
items.e: Diffusion is passive.

items.q: What do exopeptidases do?
c: hydrolyze peptide bonds in the middle of chains
remove amino acids from the ends of polypeptides
items.e: Endopeptidases act within the chain.

Why do single-celled organisms not need a gas exchange system?
c: they have a large surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion is fast enough
items.e: Larger organisms need specialized surfaces.

items.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 10 cm, as x : 1.
A block of agar is 1 cm × 4 cm × 6 cm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio, as x : 1.
How do xerophytes reduce water loss?
c: more stomata on the upper surface
sunken stomata, rolled leaves and hairs that trap moist air
items.e: These reduce the water potential gradient.

items.q: Why can insects not grow very large?
c: gases move along the tracheae mainly by diffusion, which is slow over long distances
items.e: Muscle movement can help ventilate the tracheae.

items.q: How is air carried to the cells of an insect?
items.e: Gas exchange happens at the tracheole ends.

items.q: Why are gill filaments covered in lamellae?
c: to increase the surface area for gas exchange
items.e: Each lamella has many capillaries.

items.q: What is the counter-current system in fish gills?
c: water and blood flow the same way
blood flows back into the mouth
water and blood flow in opposite directions, keeping a diffusion gradient along the whole lamella
items.e: More oxygen is absorbed than with parallel flow.

items.q: What does the trachea contain to keep it open?
items.e: The cartilage is C-shaped.

items.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 4 cm, as x : 1.
Which molecule can diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer?
items.e: Small, non-polar molecules pass easily.

items.q: Which enzyme digests starch to maltose?
items.e: Made in the salivary glands and pancreas.
